today: RFC 829 is a reference document that briefly describes packet satellite technology and lists related publications. It focuses on experimental and operational experience.

sections.title: From ALOHA to Packet Satellites
sections.content:
The RFC traces packet satellite technology to packet switching on shared radio channels at the University of Hawaii. In ALOHA, multiple terminals shared a transmit frequency, and a terminal retransmitted after a randomly chosen time if it did not receive an acknowledgement.

The RFC says researchers later demonstrated the ALOHA concept on a satellite channel linking Hawaii and NASA-Ames via ATS-1.
sections.plainLanguage: ALOHA let many radio terminals share one channel and try again if no acknowledgement arrived. The technique was later demonstrated over a satellite link.

sections.title: The SATNET Experiment
sections.content:
DARPA began developing a packet satellite system in 1973 using an INTELSAT-IV satellite and participating organizations in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Norway. The experiment shared a high-speed channel among ground stations.

SATNET underwent performance evaluations and tests during 1975–1978. The memo describes later use for international experiments and notes a ground station added for the German Aeronautics and Space Research Establishment in 1982.
sections.plainLanguage: SATNET connected ground stations through a shared satellite channel. The memo summarizes its testing, participants, and research use.

sections.title: The Reference List
sections.content:
The RFC groups papers on early ALOHA work, SATNET development and system design, operational experience, experimental results, and integration with packet networks.

The bibliography is intended for researchers interested in packet satellite experiments and operational experience with shared satellite channels.
sections.plainLanguage: The bibliography points readers to papers about how packet satellite systems were designed, tested, and operated.
